chapter_theme: Settled at Jayanti, Udayanan sinks in pleasure with Vasavadatta and forgets his lost kingdom; Yugi, reading this, plans to part the king from the queen by stratagem, sends a Sankhya woman ascetic with a portrait, and the king, after a sage's prophecy, garlands Virisikai.

cast.role: king of Vatsa, living at Jayanti with Vasavadatta
Udayanan's minister who plans to part him from the queen
Udayanan's wife, daughter of the king of Ujjain
a minister to whom Yugi tells his plan
the king of Ujjain (named by title)
the Sankhya woman ascetic, called the old woman, who carries the portrait
the sage's daughter, whom Udayanan garlands

121.reading: The poet turns to what Udayanan did after reaching Jayanti, having left Ujjain, and says he gave himself to his love for the parrot-voiced lady.
121.event: Udayanan, settled at Jayanti, turns to enjoying Vasavadatta.

122.reading: He joins the bright-jewelled lady in the sweet manner of a sacrifice and enjoys the great pleasures of the senses with her, his love growing.
122.nuance: The comparison of union to a sacrifice (வேள்வி) and to the union of the serpent-folk is the poet's own image for the richness of the pleasure; the verse does not blame it.
122.event: Udayanan enjoys the pleasures of union with Vasavadatta.

123.reading: Unable to see the shore of his desire, the elephant-lord sinks in it, and the god of love's arrows plunge him deeper, until he swims the sea of desire with the lady's breast for a raft.
123.nuance: Desire is drawn as a sea he cannot cross; the raft that keeps him afloat is the very thing that holds him in it.

124.reading: He no longer thinks of the land he lost or of his lowly state, forgets virtue and his own self, lets neither night nor day go, and the king sinks, fallen in the lady's charms and bewildered.
124.nuance: The poet blames the king's forgetting directly (மறந்து, விழுந்து), and this is what the minister's later plan answers; it is the poet's judgement, not the lover's own.
124.event: Udayanan, absorbed in Vasavadatta, forgets his lost kingdom and his duty.

claims.claim: a king who sinks in pleasure forgets his lost land and virtue

125.reading: While the king goes on like this, Yugi, dearer than life, looks on at the departure of Vatsa, freed from prison by Yugi's own scheme, with the fair lady on the young she-elephant.
125.nuance: Lines 1 and 4 can be read as Yugi watching the flight or as the poet recalling it; the grammar of the verse is loose.
125.event: Yugi, having freed the king from prison by his scheme, watches him ride off with the lady.

126.reading: Yugi, thinking lovingly of returning, hears that the king of Ujjain is grieving inwardly, learns by stratagem that the great army has not risen, leaves Ujjain's bounds and goes to Pushpakam.
126.nuance: The king of Ujjain is named only by title (உஞ்சைநகர்க் கரசன்); his grief at the escape is told, not shown.
126.event: Yugi, learning that Ujjain's army has not moved, leaves its border and goes to Pushpakam.

127.reading: Yugi tells Idabakan his own purpose and asks what effort is now fitting for their golden-crowned king; and as he comes on a she-elephant and has crossed a wide land, the elephant cannot bear to step and falls to the ground.
127.nuance: Lines 3 to 4 seem to recall the she-elephant's fall already told in verse 114, mixed into Yugi's talk; the verse's order of events is not clear.
127.event: Yugi confides his plan to Idabakan; the she-elephant on which the king rides collapses.

128.reading: A list of what befell: the hunters closed round them, the king beat them, he went with the matchless Vayantakan, entered Jayanti with its white flags, and joined the lady in love.
128.nuance: Only a string of nouns in -ததும்; who recites the list, the poet or Yugi, is not stated.
128.event: The verse recalls the hunters' siege, the king's victory and arrival at Jayanti.

129.reading: Hearing that the king, absorbed in pleasure, thinks nothing of the land he lost, Yugi smiles, his teeth shining, and decides that if the king is parted from his queen by a trick, the lost kingdom will come back to his hand.
129.nuance: Yugi's reasoning is given as his own thought (எண்ணினான்); the poem has not yet shown whether the plan is wise.
129.event: Yugi plans to part the king from the queen by stratagem in order to win back the kingdom.

claims.claim: a king's lost rule is recovered only if he is drawn out of his pleasure by stratagem

130.reading: Yugi meets a woman ascetic of the Sankhya school, tells her what to say, and, as if his own life had left him, paints on a cloth the three ministers and the king's form.
130.nuance: The word சாங்கிய is used only to name the woman's order; the verse states no Sankhya doctrine.
130.event: Yugi instructs a Sankhya woman ascetic and has a portrait made of the king and his ministers.

131.reading: One figure in the portrait is set with the upper eye wide and the left one removed; with this and a message to be made known to the crowned king, the old woman goes and sees the lion-voiced lord.
131.nuance: Lines 1 to 2 on the painted eye are hard to parse; what the missing eye signals is not clear from the verse.
131.event: The old woman takes the portrait to Udayanan.

132.reading: The king sees her and, wishing to honour her, bids her sit; the kinswoman speaks kindly and then asks why Yugi, who freed him from prison, has not come back with him, and bids him tell.
132.event: The old woman asks Udayanan why Yugi did not return with him.

133.reading: The king has no word of Yugi, so the seated woman shows him the portrait; the king sees it, laments and grieves much, and then bows to a sage rich in penance and asks him.
133.event: The old woman shows the portrait; Udayanan laments, then bows to a sage and asks him.

134.reading: The sage assures him firmly that he will regain his crowned rule and his companion in bodily form; the king, trusting this, garlands the slender-waisted Virisikai, the sage's daughter he sees in the scented hill-slope.
134.nuance: The verse does not make clear whether the garlanding is part of the sage's counsel or a separate act; the prophecy is told by the poet, in the sage's words only in sense.
134.event: A sage foretells Udayanan's return of rule and friend; Udayanan then garlands the sage's daughter Virisikai.

135.reading: He unites with her, and when she is called away to the forest by her friends and the king goes, Yugi, in his mind, appears to the king to part the queen from him for some days.
135.nuance: The last line is not clear; it can be read as Yugi's thought of parting the queen or as his appearance for that purpose.
135.event: After the union, Udayanan leaves, and Yugi sets about parting the king from the queen for some days.

links.note: Yugi's plan in verse 129 answers the king's forgetting of his lost land in verse 124.
links.teaches: The poet first blames the king's neglect and then shows who will act on it, so the neglect becomes the cause of the plot that follows.

links.note: Yugi's briefing of the ascetic and the portrait carry out the plan he forms in verse 129.
links.teaches: The plan to part the king from the queen is not carried by Yugi's own presence but by a woman and a picture, so the stratagem works through trust in others.

links.note: The portrait the old woman carries in verse 131 is the one she shows the king in verse 133.
links.teaches: What the portrait is for is clear only when the king sees it and breaks into grief, so the picture works as a message that needs no word.

links.note: The king, after seeing the portrait in verse 133, asks the sage whose answer verse 134 gives.
links.teaches: The king's grief turns not to action but to a sage's assurance, so the answer to Yugi's lure is a prophecy that makes him wait.

links.note: Verse 135 shows Yugi appearing to part the queen from the king, as planned in verse 129.
links.teaches: The plan formed in smiling thought is now set in motion after the king has taken a second bride, so Yugi's scheme and the king's new love run side by side.

links.note: Kural 901 says desire for a wife costs a man what action needs; Yugi concludes the same of the king's union, and cures it by a stratagem, not by the king's restraint.
links.teaches: The couplet speaks to the man who must resist his own desire, while the epic gives the cure to a minister who engineers an absence.

gains.a: The epic scene gains a general rule that makes the king's fault a known failing of men intent on pleasure, not only his own.
gains.b: The couplet gains a case in which the fault is not mended by the husband's restraint but by an outside plan, which the couplet never considers.

links.note: Kural 638 makes it the minister's duty to tell a king what is good for him; Yugi, given a king who will not hear, chooses a trick.
links.teaches: The couplet assumes the king can be told, while the poem shows a minister who judges telling useless and acts in secret.

gains.a: The epic scene gains the name of a duty that Yugi both keeps in aim and breaks in method.
gains.b: The couplet gains a case where the minister's duty to speak is overtaken by deceit for the king's own good.

links.note: Kural 539 bids a man remember the ruined when swollen with joy; the king of verse 124 forgets even his own ruin.
links.teaches: The couplet's remedy needs a remembering mind, and the poem shows the king in whom nothing remains to be reminded.

gains.a: The verse gains the couplet's name for the fault: joy that swells past remembering.
gains.b: The couplet gains a king whose own loss, not another's, is the ruin he forgets.

links.note: Verse 123 calls the lady's breast a raft in the sea of desire; Naladiyar 17 warns that the same woman will one day walk bent on a staff.
links.teaches: The epic's rapture and the quatrain's warning use the same woman and cannot both be the last word on her.

gains.a: The epic's image of desire as a sea gains a bounded end in the quatrain's picture of age.
gains.b: The quatrain's warning gains a living king who does not heed it and pays with his land.

source_issues: Verses 125, 127 and 128: the order of events and the speaker are not clear.
Verse 131 lines 1 to 2: the painted eye and its sense are hard to read.
Verse 135 line 4: the grammar is loose, so Yugi's role in the parting is uncertain.
